newsitem.title: ESTONIA: INTERVIEW-ESTONIAN TELEPHONE TO BE 50 PCT DIGITAL 1999.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-ESTONIAN TELEPHONE TO BE 50 PCT DIGITAL 1999.

text.p: Estonia's telecommunications operator, Estonian Telephone Co Ltd, said on Tuesday its network would be 50 percent digital by early 1999.

Chief executive Jaan Mannik said the company, that is 51 percent state owned and 24.5 percent owned by Swedish operator Telia and by Telecom Finland, would be over 30 percent digital by the end of this year.
"Our aim is to be 90 percent digital by 2004," Mannik told Reuters in an interview.
Mannik said Estonian Telephone Co, that was set up in 1992 with a monopoly on basic voice services in Estonia until 2001, was growing rapidly.
"The growth has been faster than predicted in 1992," said Mannik, a former Telia employee who took over leadership of the Estonian company at the start of 1997.
"The development of the country goes hand-in-hand with the development of the telecommunications sector and vice versa. This stronger growth is due to Estonian's strong economic growth."
Turnover in the company is rising steadily, reaching 800 million kroons last year and expected to reach one billion kroons this year.
Much of this is put back into the company with 655 million kroons to be invested in extending and renewing lines and infrastrucutre this year.
In 1996 Estonia Telephone spent 528 million kroons on this work and in 1995 400 million kroons.
"We are extending and renewing 15 percent of the network each year," Mannik said.
"With this size of investment we are by far the largest investor in Estonia."
Following the strong growth, Estonian Telephone now has 450,000 customers with a waiting list of over 100,000.
To keep up with the rapid growth the company is building 50,000 new lines each year and converting up to 25,000 old lines to new technology a year.
"Within four years this queue should be gone," said Mannik.

Mannik said foreign companies were already starting to show an interest in Estonia's telecoms sector even though the monopoly on voice services will remain in place until 2001 as outlined in a 1992 government concession that received European Union approval.

The company's mobile operator, Estonian Mobile Telephone Co Ltd, which is also owned 51 percent by the state and 24.5 percent by both Telia and Telecom Finland but run separately, already had two competitors, one from Finland and one partly from the U.S..
Several companies were vying for the data services market and the number of Internet providers is already over 10.
"As in other countries in Europe, foreign companies are starting to move in and find themselves a position in the market," Mannik said.
"But this competition can be healthy in a growing sector like this."
